questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Indicate the type of reasoning used in this argument: *since African countries are under developed and Cameroon is an African Country, it means that she is under developed.*

(ii) Criticize this Definition, *An engineer is one who performs engineering activities.* (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The reasoning goes from a general truth ("African countries are underdeveloped") applied to a particular case ("Cameroon is an African country") to a particular conclusion ("Cameroon is underdeveloped"): it is **deductive reasoning** (a categorical syllogism of the form All M are P; S is M; therefore S is P). The conclusion is as certain as the premises. (Remark: the general premise is itself doubtful, but the type of reasoning is deductive.)

**(ii)** The definition **is circular** (it commits the fault of "defining a term by itself"): the word defined, "engineer", reappears in the defining part as "engineering". It therefore explains nothing to someone who does not already know what an engineer is. A good definition must not contain the term to be defined (nor a synonym or a derivative of it) and must be clearer than the term defined. A correct definition would be: "An engineer is a professional who designs, builds and maintains machines, structures or systems by applying scientific and mathematical knowledge."
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
O Level Logic - definition and division

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Using *mothers* as Subject Term and *caring persons* as the Predicate Term, construct an O Standard Form Categorical Proposition.

(ii) Determine the Distribution of Terms in the Proposition in b (i) above. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** An **O** proposition is particular negative: "Some S are not P". With S = mothers and P = caring persons:

**Some mothers are not caring persons.**

**(ii) Distribution.** In an O proposition the **subject term is undistributed** (only some mothers are in question) and the **predicate term is distributed** (the mothers concerned are excluded from the whole class of caring persons). So "mothers" is **undistributed** and "caring persons" is **distributed**.
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Determine the validity of the Syllogism below using the General rules of the Categorical Syllogism:

*No pastors are liars*

*Some prophets are not pastors.*

*Therefore, some prophets are not liars*

(ii) Give the Converse of, *No Spirits are mortals:* (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Terms: major term "liars", minor term "prophets", middle term "pastors". Propositions: E, O, O. The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: first figure, so the syllogism is **EOO-1**.

General rules:
- Middle term distributed at least once: "pastors" is distributed in the E premise: satisfied.
- A term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in the premise: "liars" (predicate of the O conclusion) is distributed, and it is distributed in the premise (predicate of an E): satisfied; "prophets" is undistributed in the conclusion: satisfied.
- **No conclusion can be drawn from two negative premises**: here both premises are negative (E and O): **this rule is broken**, which is the fallacy of **exclusive premises**.
- A negative premise requires a negative conclusion: satisfied.

**The syllogism is invalid** (a full check of all the possible cases confirms that EOO-1 is invalid): from "No pastors are liars" and "Some prophets are not pastors", nothing follows about whether the prophets are liars or not.

**(ii) Converse.** Conversion exchanges the subject and the predicate and keeps the quality. An E proposition converts simply:

**No mortals are spirits.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Construct an Enthymeme of the Second Order from the Syllogism in c (i) above

*No women are priests.*

*Some priests are teachers.*

*Therefore, some teachers are not women.*

(ii) Identify the form of this Argument

*If the questions are easy then the students will pass the exams.*

*Questions are easy.*

*Therefore, students will pass the exams.* (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A second-order enthymeme is a syllogism whose **minor premise is suppressed** (understood but not stated). The minor premise of the syllogism is "Some priests are teachers" (it contains the minor term "teachers"). The enthymeme of the second order is therefore:

**No women are priests; therefore, some teachers are not women.** (Understood: "Some priests are teachers.")

(The syllogism itself is valid: EIO in the fourth figure, EIO-4.)

**(ii) Form.** The first premise is a conditional, the second affirms its antecedent and the conclusion affirms its consequent: this is the **modus ponens** (affirming the antecedent), the valid form of the **mixed hypothetical syllogism**: $p \supset q$, $p$, $\therefore q$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) Construct the Truth-Table for $(\sim p \cdot \sim q)$

(ii) Symbolize this statement using the variables p and q, *neither teachers nor students are illiterates.* (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Compute $\sim p$ and $\sim q$ first, then their conjunction:

| $p$ | $q$ | $\sim p$ | $\sim q$ | $\sim p \cdot \sim q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | T | T |

The expression is true only when $p$ and $q$ are both false (it is contingent).

**(ii)** Let $p$ = teachers are illiterates and $q$ = students are illiterates. "Neither ... nor" means "not the first and not the second":

$$\sim p \cdot \sim q$$

(equivalent to $\sim (p \vee q)$).
